title: For Sheikh Iftikhar Ahmad Naseem
takeaway: Death isn't the end for good people. It's the road to real life.
scene: An elegy for Sheikh Iftikhar Ahmad Naseem, a poet friend who wrote naats, poems in praise of the Prophet. The poet plays on his pen-name: 'Naseem' means a gentle breeze.

original: ایس فانی جہان توں جان والے، پھیرا فیر نہ آپ نے پاؤنا ایں
نیک لوکاں نوں جگ اے یاد کردا، عمل نیک کم حشر نوں آؤنا ایں
transliteration: Is faani jahaan ton jaan vaale, phera pher na aap ne paauna ain
Nek lokaan nu jag ae yaad karda, amal nek kam hashr nu aauna ain
translation: You who are leaving this passing world will never come back to visit.
The world remembers good people, and good deeds will count on the Day of Judgment.
couplets.story: His friend has left this temporary world and won't be coming back. The world remembers good people, and the good things they did will count when God judges everyone.

original: شعر ادب دا رہے گا باغ کھڑیا ایتھے بلبلاں چہ چہاؤنا ایں
سدا وگے گی باد نسیم احمدؔ، ساڈا یار نسیم نہ آؤنا ایں
transliteration: Shair adab da rahe ga baagh khiriya, ethe bulbulaan chah chahaauna ain
Sada vage gi baad-e-naseem Ahmad, saada yaar Naseem na aauna ain
translation: The garden of poetry and literature will stay in bloom, and nightingales will sing here.
Ahmad, the gentle breeze (naseem) will always blow, but our friend Naseem won't come back.
couplets.story: The world of poetry will keep blooming, and new 'nightingales' will keep singing. Then a sad play on words: the gentle breeze, 'naseem', will always blow, but their friend Naseem won't return.

original: توں موت دے مونہہ وچ جا کے وی، رستہ اصل حیاتی دا پا گیا ایں
سنن واسطے حوراں بیتاب ہوسن نعتاں ایتھے جو توں سنا گیا ایں
transliteration: Toon maut de moonh vich ja ke vi, rasta asl hayaati da pa gaya ain
Sunan vaaste hooraan betaab hosan, naataan ethe jo toon suna gaya ain
translation: Even going into the jaws of death, you found the road to real life.
The maidens of paradise will be eager to hear the naats you recited here.
couplets.story: Even though he died, he found the way to true life, the life that comes after this one. The poet imagines heaven's companions waiting eagerly to hear the poems about the Prophet that Naseem used to recite on earth.

original: نسیمؔ جنت چ اعلیٰ مقام تیرا، بوٹے ادب تے نیکی دے لا گیا ایں
احمدؔ غماں دا زور نہ جھل ہووے، ایسے کرب دے جھکھڑ جھلا گیا ایں
transliteration: Naseem jannat ch aala muqaam tera, boote adab te neki de la gaya ain
Ahmad ghamaan da zor na jhal hove, aise karb de jhakhar jhula gaya ain
translation: Naseem, your place in paradise is high; you planted the saplings of literature and goodness.
Ahmad can't bear the weight of this grief; you've set such storms of pain blowing.
couplets.story: He believes Naseem has a high place in paradise, because he planted seeds of poetry and kindness. But the poet himself can barely handle the grief. Losing his friend has started a storm of pain.

deeper: This elegy holds the Islamic view of death clearly. Death is not an end but 'the road to real life', and good deeds are carried into the next world. The poet imagines his friend's naats being heard in paradise, which shows how much devotion to the Prophet meant to their circle.
why: It's a gentle, hopeful way of thinking about death: the people we lose can be going somewhere better.
prompt: What good 'saplings' would you like to plant that could keep growing after you're gone?
